title: Jerusalem
author: Selma Lagerlöf
openingText: A young farmer was plowing his field one summer morning. The sun shone, the grass sparkled with dew, and the air was so light and bracing that no words can describe it. The horses were frisky from the morning air, and pulled the plow along as if in play. Why is it that I feel so discouraged at times and think life so hard? What more does one want than sunshine and fair weather to be as happy as a child of Heaven?
about:
Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion is William Blake's longest and most ambitious illuminated book — about 100 plates of poetry and engraved illustration. It tells of the fall of Albion (Britain personified) into a state of selfishness and division, and his final reunification with Jerusalem, who represents spiritual liberty. The poem is dense, mythological, and unlike anything else in English.

Blake worked on Jerusalem from around 1804 to 1820. He wrote it, engraved it, hand-colored each copy, and sold the few he made personally. The poem was almost unread in his lifetime. It has since been recognized as one of the most original works in the language.

angleCards.title: Land versus conviction.
angleCards.text: The Ingmarssons have farmed the same land for generations. Hellgum's gospel asks them to sell it. I want to read the novel as an argument about what a person owes the place they were born to, and what is lost when rootedness gives way to belief.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jerusalem as an argument about land and conviction — what a person owes the place they come from, and what is lost when a new faith asks them to give it up.

angleCards.title: A real religious awakening.
angleCards.text: Lagerlöf based the pilgrimage on real events — the Nås colony of 1896. I want to treat the novel as a study of how a charismatic preacher actually splits a community, and whether Lagerlöf is sympathetic to the awakening or critical of it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jerusalem to understand how a real religious awakening works from the inside — how Hellgum convinces ordinary people to give up everything, and where Lagerlöf's own judgment falls.

angleCards.title: The Ingmar line and its burden.
angleCards.text: Young Ingmar inherits both the farm and the family's long, rigid sense of duty — the weight of what every Ingmar before him has done. I want to read the novel as a portrait of inheritance: what it means to carry a name, and what it costs to honour it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jerusalem as a story about inheritance — about what it means to carry a family name like Ingmarsson, and the quiet cost of living up to the people who came before.

angleCards.title: Women holding the centre.
angleCards.text: Karin, Gertrud, Brita — the novel's women carry the weight of the decisions, often more than the men do. I want to track how Lagerlöf writes them: what they give up, what they choose, and what she is saying about where conviction and endurance actually live.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jerusalem to pay close attention to its women — Karin, Gertrud, Brita — and to understand what Lagerlöf is saying about who in this world actually bears the weight of belief and choice.

cast.name: Ingmar Ingmarsson the Younger
cast.description: Inherits the farm, the name, and the family's long expectation of quiet duty. In love with Gertrud. The novel follows what it costs him to be an Ingmar at a moment when the world is asking the Ingmarssons to become something else.

cast.name: Karin Ingmarsdotter
cast.description: Ingmar's older sister, married into the farm's future and then drawn into Hellgum's movement. One of the first to believe, and one of those who gives up the most. Her conviction is the novel's strongest single force.

cast.name: Halvor Halvorsson
cast.description: A merchant who marries into the Ingmar family and then follows Karin into the new faith. Steady, practical, and willing to liquidate a life's work when he is persuaded. His loyalty is one of the novel's quietest miracles.

cast.name: Hellgum
cast.description: Arrives from Chicago preaching a new gospel of community, holiness, and departure. Splits the village in two. Not a villain and not a saint — a man whose certainty is powerful enough to reshape other people's entire lives.

cast.name: Gertrud
cast.description: The girl Ingmar loves — also drawn into Hellgum's orbit. Her pull between ordinary love and spiritual calling is one of the novel's central aches, and one of the clearest places where the whole story's question becomes personal.

cast.name: Strong Ingmar
cast.description: The old Ingmar of the previous generation — embodiment of the family's traditional authority and peasant wisdom. What he represents does not survive the book intact, and the novel asks what replaces him, and whether anything can.

whyItMatters.title: A Self-Made Mythology
whyItMatters.body: Blake invented his own mythology — Albion, Los, Urizen, Vala — to think with. Few poets have ever attempted this; fewer still have made it work. Reading Jerusalem is encountering a coherent symbolic universe assembled by one mind.

whyItMatters.title: The Engraved Book as Form
whyItMatters.body: Blake did not just write Jerusalem — he engraved every plate and printed it himself. The visual and textual elements are inseparable. The poem is one of the great experiments in book as art object, and reading it without the images is reading half the work.

whyItMatters.title: The Liberation of Imagination
whyItMatters.body: The poem argues that what enslaves humans is not material conditions but the failure of imagination — the willingness to mistake reason for the whole of mind. Blake's defense of imagination as the root of human freedom remains one of the most concentrated in literature.
